pages.title: Part 1: The Phosphagen System and Cellular Energy Resynthesis
pages.readingHtml:
The Phosphagen System and Cellular Energy Resynthesis

Three basic energy systems exist in mammalian skeletal muscle cells to replenish adenosine triphosphate (ATP): the phosphagen system, glycolysis, and the oxidative system. In exercise bioenergetics, metabolic pathways are categorized into anaerobic (oxygen-independent) processes occurring in the cell sarcoplasm and aerobic (oxygen-dependent) processes occurring in the mitochondria. The phosphagen and glycolytic pathways operate anaerobically, whereas the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain (ETC) function aerobically, requiring molecular oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor. Of the three primary macronutrients—carbohydrate, protein, and fat—only carbohydrate can be metabolized for energy without the direct involvement of oxygen.

Phosphagen System Kinematics and Kinetics

The phosphagen system provides ATP primarily for short-term, high-intensity activities (e.g., maximal sprinting and heavy resistance training) and is highly active at the onset of all exercise regardless of intensity. This system relies on cellular ATP hydrolysis and the breakdown of creatine phosphate (CP), also termed phosphocreatine (PCr). The reversible enzyme creatine kinase catalyzes the synthesis of ATP from CP and adenosine diphosphate (ADP):

ADP + CP ↔ ATP + Creatine (catalyzed by Creatine Kinase)

Skeletal muscle stores relatively small amounts of CP, limiting its capacity as a continuous primary energy supplier for long-duration activities. Under normal resting conditions, muscle CP concentrations are 4 to 6 times higher than ATP concentrations (80 to 100 g or ~3 oz of total body ATP). Resting ATP stores cannot be completely depleted during fatigue, typically decreasing by only 50% to 60% of preexercise levels to maintain baseline cellular viability. Type II (fast-twitch) muscle fibers contain significantly higher CP concentrations than Type I (slow-twitch) fibers, enabling individuals with higher Type II composition to resynthesize ATP faster during high-power anaerobic performance.

Adenylate Kinase Reaction and Law of Mass Action

Another single-enzyme reaction that rapidly replenishes ATP is catalyzed by adenylate kinase (also termed myokinase):

2 ADP ↔ ATP + AMP (catalyzed by Adenylate Kinase)

The product adenosine monophosphate (AMP) is a powerful allosteric activator of glycolytic enzymes. The reactions of the phosphagen system are regulated by the law of mass action (mass action effect), which states that the concentrations of reactants or products in solution drive the direction of enzyme-mediated reactions. Accumulation of sarcoplasmic ADP and Pi drives creatine kinase and adenylate kinase forward to restore ATP equilibrium.

Coaching /Sport Application

High-power events lasting under 6 seconds (e.g., 100m sprint start, Olympic weightlifting) depend strictly on phosphagen capacity. Rest intervals between maximal resistance training sets must be structured long enough (2 to 5 minutes) to permit substantial CP repletion driven by mass action kinetics.

Phosphagen SystemSarcoplasmCreatine Phosphate (CP) / ADPHighest Rate / Lowest Capacity
Adenylate Kinase ReactionSarcoplasmADP + ADPImmediate Rate / Very Low Capacity

pages.title: Part 2: Glycolysis, Lactate Formation, and Metabolic Acidosis
pages.readingHtml:
Glycolysis, Lactate Formation, and Metabolic Acidosis

Glycolysis is the breakdown of carbohydrate—either muscle glycogen or blood glucose—to resynthesize ATP via a series of enzymatic reactions in the sarcoplasm. Because glycolysis involves multiple enzymatic steps, its rate of ATP resynthesis is slower than the single-step phosphagen system; however, its overall capacity is substantially greater due to larger intracellular glycogen stores.

The Dual Fates of Pyruvate

Pyruvate represents the ultimate end product of glycolysis. Its metabolic fate is governed primarily by cellular energy demand and oxygen availability within the mitochondria:

  • Anaerobic Glycolysis (Fast Glycolysis): When energy demand is high and must be transferred rapidly, pyruvate is converted to lactate in the sarcoplasm by lactate dehydrogenase. This path rapidly regenerates NAD+ to maintain high glycolytic throughput, though duration is limited by accompanying intracellular proton accumulation.
  • Aerobic Glycolysis (Slow Glycolysis): When energy demand is moderate and oxygen is sufficient, pyruvate is transported into the mitochondria along with NADH and converted to acetyl-CoA for entry into the Krebs cycle.

Debunking the Lactic Acid Myth & Metabolic Acidosis

A common misnomer in exercise physiology is that glycolysis produces 'lactic acid' that dissociates into lactate and H+. At physiological pH (~7.0), the phosphoglycerate kinase step leaves a carboxylate group (COO-), producing lactate directly without a dissociable proton. Furthermore, the conversion of pyruvate to lactate actually consumes H+ ions, acting as a temporary metabolic buffer rather than the cause of acidosis.

Intracellular proton accumulation—termed metabolic acidosis—stems primarily from ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O → ADP + Pi + H+). Accumulating H+ decreases cytosolic pH, inhibiting glycolytic enzyme activity, impairing crossbridge recycling, and interfering with excitation-contraction coupling by competing with Ca2+ for troponin binding sites.

Lactate Dynamics and the Cori Cycle

Resting blood lactate concentration ranges between 0.5 to 2.2 mmol/L. Maximal lactate production rate is twice as high in Type II muscle fibers (0.5 mmol·g-1·s-1) compared to Type I fibers (0.25 mmol·g-1·s-1). Lactate cleared from skeletal muscle is oxidized locally or transported via the bloodstream to the liver, where it is converted to glucose via gluconeogenesis in the Cori cycle.

Coaching /Sport Application

Active recovery (light low-intensity movement) significantly enhances post-exercise blood lactate clearance compared to passive rest by enhancing muscular lactate oxidation and hepatic Cori cycle flux.

Glycolytic PathwayPyruvate End-ProductRate of ATP SynthesisDuration Potential
Fast (Anaerobic) GlycolysisLactate (Sarcoplasm)RapidShort to Medium (30–90 s)
Slow (Aerobic) GlycolysisAcetyl-CoA (Mitochondria)SlowerExtended (>2 min)

pages.title: Part 3: Glycolytic Bioenergetics, Energy Yield, Regulation, and Lactate Thresholds
pages.readingHtml:
Glycolytic Bioenergetics, Energy Yield, Regulation, and Lactate Thresholds

The net chemical reaction for fast glycolysis converting glucose to lactate is expressed as:

Glucose + 2 Pi + 2 ADP → 2 Lactate + 2 ATP + H2O

When pyruvate is shuttled into the mitochondria for aerobic processing, the net glycolytic reaction is:

Glucose + 2 Pi + 2 ADP + 2 NAD+ → 2 Pyruvate + 2 ATP + 2 NADH + 2 H2O

Substrate-Level Phosphorylation and Net ATP Yield

ATP resynthesis during metabolism occurs via substrate-level phosphorylation (direct transfer of phosphate from substrate to ADP) or oxidative phosphorylation (resynthesis in the mitochondrial electron transport chain). Glycolysis produces a gross total of 4 ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation (catalyzed by phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase). However, net yield depends on the substrate origin:

  • Blood Glucose: Hexokinase hydrolyzes 1 ATP to phosphorylate glucose to glucose-6-phosphate; PFK hydrolyzes a 2nd ATP. Net yield = 4 - 2 = 2 ATP.
  • Muscle Glycogen: Glycogenolysis catalyzed by glycogen phosphorylase yields pre-phosphorylated glucose. Only 1 ATP (PFK step) is hydrolyzed. Net yield = 4 - 1 = 3 ATP.

Allosteric Regulation of Key Enzymes

Glycolysis is regulated by three key enzymes possessing allosteric binding sites:

  • Hexokinase: Allosterically inhibited by its product, glucose-6-phosphate.
  • Phosphofructokinase (PFK): The primary rate-limiting step of glycolysis. Allosterically inhibited by high ATP, CP, citrate, and free fatty acids; allosterically activated by AMP, ADP, Pi, and ammonia.
  • Pyruvate Kinase: Inhibited by ATP and acetyl-CoA; activated by AMP and fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.

Lactate Threshold (LT) and OBLA

The lactate threshold (LT) marks the exercise intensity at which blood lactate begins an abrupt increase above baseline, signaling increased reliance on anaerobic mechanisms. LT occurs at 50% to 60% of V̇O2max in untrained individuals and 70% to 80% in aerobically trained athletes. A second inflection point, the onset of blood lactate accumulation (OBLA), occurs when blood lactate concentration reaches 4 mmol/L.

Coaching /Sport Application

Training at or slightly above LT/OBLA induces physiological adaptations—such as increased mitochondrial density and reduced catecholamine secretion—that shift the lactate curve to the right, allowing athletes to sustain higher power outputs without premature acidosis.

Blood Glucose2 ATP4 ATP2 ATP
Muscle Glycogen1 ATP4 ATP3 ATP

pages.title: Part 4: The Oxidative System and Substrate Oxidation
pages.readingHtml:
The Oxidative System and Substrate Oxidation

The oxidative system is the primary source of ATP at rest and during low-intensity steady-state exercise. At rest, approximately 70% of ATP is derived from fat oxidation and 30% from carbohydrate oxidation. As exercise intensity increases, substrate utilization shifts preferentially toward carbohydrates. During submaximal, prolonged exercise (>90 minutes), fuel selection gradually shifts back toward fat oxidation.

Glucose and Glycogen Oxidation Pathways

When oxygen is present, pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix and is converted to acetyl-CoA by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. Acetyl-CoA enters the Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle), where substrate-level phosphorylation produces 2 GTP (equivalent to 2 ATP) per glucose molecule. The oxidation of substrate also yields 6 NADH and 2 FADH2 from the Krebs cycle (plus 2 NADH from glycolysis and 2 NADH from pyruvate conversion).

These reduced coenzymes transfer hydrogen protons and electrons to the electron transport chain (ETC) across cytochromes. Oxygen acts as the final electron acceptor, forming H2O. Each NADH yields 3 ATP, whereas each FADH2 yields 2 ATP. Complete oxidative degradation of 1 molecule of blood glucose yields approximately 38 ATP (39 ATP from muscle glycogen). Oxidative phosphorylation accounts for >90% of total cellular ATP resynthesis.

Fat Oxidation and Beta Oxidation

Triglycerides in adipose tissue or intramuscular stores are hydrolyzed by hormone-sensitive lipase into glycerol and free fatty acids. Free fatty acids enter the mitochondria to undergo beta oxidation—a cyclic cascade breaking fatty acid chains into acetyl-CoA, NADH, and FADH2. Beta oxidation of a single triglyceride containing three 16-carbon palmitic acid chains yields over 300 ATP molecules, demonstrating fat oxidation's immense capacity.

Protein Oxidation and Regulation

Protein is a minor energy substrate (3% to 18% during prolonged exercise). Amino acids are converted via gluconeogenesis into glucose, pyruvate, or Krebs cycle intermediates. Skeletal muscle oxidizes mainly branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs)—leucine, isoleucine, and valine. Nitrogenous waste is eliminated as urea and toxic ammonia. The rate-limiting enzyme of the Krebs cycle is isocitrate dehydrogenase, inhibited by ATP and activated by ADP.

Coaching /Sport Application

Aerobic endurance training increases mitochondrial volume and oxidative enzyme density, enhancing fat oxidation capacity at submaximal workloads and sparing limited muscle glycogen stores for high-intensity surges.

Substrate CategoryPrimary Metabolic PathwayATP RateTotal ATP Yield Capacity
Carbohydrate (Glucose)Glycolysis + Krebs + ETCModerate38–39 ATP per molecule
Fat (Triglyceride)Beta Oxidation + Krebs + ETCSlowest>300 ATP per molecule
Protein (BCAAs)Deamination + Krebs / GluconeogenesisSlowestVariable (3%–18% total energy)

pages.title: Part 5: Energy Production Rates, Capacity, and Exercise Specificity
pages.readingHtml:
Energy Production Rates, Capacity, and Exercise Specificity

The three biological energy systems exhibit a fundamental inverse relationship between their maximum rate of ATP production (ATP resynthesized per unit time) and their total capacity (total ATP produced over time). High power output demands a rapid energy supply, relying on pathways with high rates and low capacities. Conversely, low-intensity, long-duration work relies on systems with immense capacities but slower production rates.

Comparative Bioenergetic Characteristics

Energy SystemMax Rate of ATP ProductionCapacity of ATP Production
Phosphagen1 (Highest / Fastest)5 (Lowest / Least)
Fast Glycolysis24
Slow Glycolysis33
Oxidation of Carbs42
Oxidation of Fats/Proteins5 (Slowest)1 (Highest / Greatest)

Exercise Intensity and Duration Interactions

The primary determinant of energy system selection is exercise intensity (quantified as power output or work per unit time), while exercise duration acts as a secondary modifier:

  • 0 to 6 seconds (Extremely High Intensity): Phosphagen system dominant.
  • 6 to 30 seconds (Very High Intensity): Phosphagen and fast glycolysis.
  • 30 seconds to 2 minutes (High Intensity): Fast glycolysis dominant.
  • 2 to 3 minutes (Moderate Intensity): Fast glycolysis and oxidative system.
  • >3 minutes (Low Intensity): Oxidative energy system dominant.
Coaching /Sport Application

At no time during rest or exercise does a single energy system provide 100% of cellular energy. Strength and conditioning coaches must prescribe work-to-rest ratios matching the targeted sport's dominant bioenergetic continuum to optimize performance adaptation.

glossary.def: The flow of energy in a biological system; concerns primarily the conversion of macronutrients into biologically usable forms of energy.
Processes that do not require the presence of oxygen.
Mechanisms that depend on oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor.
An anaerobic energy system that relies on ATP hydrolysis and creatine phosphate breakdown to rapidly resynthesize ATP for short-term, high-intensity exercise.
A high-energy phosphate molecule used by the phosphagen system to rapidly rephosphorylate ADP to ATP; also called phosphocreatine (PCr).
The enzyme that catalyzes the synthesis of ATP from CP and ADP.
An enzyme that catalyzes the single-step reaction 2ADP <-> ATP + AMP to rapidly resynthesize ATP; also called myokinase.
The principle stating that the concentrations of reactants or products (or both) in solution will drive the direction of enzyme-mediated reactions.
The breakdown of carbohydrate—either glycogen stored in the muscle or glucose delivered in the blood—to resynthesize ATP.
The end product of glycolysis, which can either be converted to lactate in the sarcoplasm or shuttled into the mitochondria.
The anion resulting from the lactate dehydrogenase reaction during fast glycolysis; serves as a metabolic buffer and energy substrate.
The enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of pyruvate to lactate in the sarcoplasm.
An exercise-induced decrease in cytosolic pH caused primarily by proton accumulation from ATP hydrolysis.
The formation of glucose from noncarbohydrate sources, such as lactate, glycerol, or amino acids.
The metabolic pathway in which lactate produced by anaerobic glycolysis in muscle is transported to the liver and converted back to glucose.
The direct resynthesis of ATP from ADP during a single reaction in metabolic pathways without requiring oxygen or electron transport.
The resynthesis of ATP from ADP occurring in the electron transport chain using proton gradients generated by substrate oxidation.
The enzymatic breakdown of stored glycogen into glucose-1-phosphate by glycogen phosphorylase.
The key regulatory, rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis that catalyzes the conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.
Regulation of an enzyme's activity occurring when a regulatory molecule binds to an allosteric ('other site') on the enzyme.
The exercise intensity at which blood lactate begins an abrupt increase above baseline concentration, indicating an increased reliance on anaerobic mechanisms.
The point during exercise of increasing intensity at which blood lactate reaches a concentration of 4 mmol/L.
The primary aerobic source of ATP at rest and during low-intensity activities, using carbohydrates, fats, and proteins as substrates.
A series of mitochondrial chemical reactions that continues the oxidation of acetyl-CoA and produces GTP, NADH, and FADH2.
A series of electron carrier proteins in the inner mitochondrial membrane that uses NADH and FADH2 to produce ATP via oxidative phosphorylation.
A series of mitochondrial reactions in which free fatty acids are broken down into acetyl-CoA, NADH, and FADH2.
An enzyme that breaks down stored triglycerides into free fatty acids and glycerol.
Essential amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine) oxidized primarily within skeletal muscle during exercise.
The primary rate-limiting enzyme of the Krebs cycle, stimulated by ADP and inhibited by ATP.
